questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: 10 plants got fertilizer and 10 did not (randomly assigned). Fertilized plants grew 2.9 cm more on average. The histogram shows 200 re-randomized differences under the model that fertilizer has no effect. Use a one-sided count (2.9 cm or more) and a 5% cutoff. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.prompt_markup: 10 plants got fertilizer and 10 did not (randomly assigned). Fertilized plants grew 2.9 cm more on average. The histogram shows 200 re-randomized differences under the model that fertilizer has no effect. Use a one-sided count (2.9 cm or more) and a 5% cutoff. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: Most re-randomized differences were near 0, so the observed difference is not significant.
4 of 200 (2%) were 2 cm or more, so the observed difference of 2.9 cm is not significant.
0 of 200 were 2.9 cm or more; 0% < 5%, so the difference is significant: fertilizer appears to increase growth.
0 of 200 were 2.9 cm or more, so this difference has probability exactly 0 and fertilizer is proved to work.

questions.correct_answer: 0 of 200 were 2.9 cm or more; 0% < 5%, so the difference is significant: fertilizer appears to increase growth.
questions.grading_note: The ≥ 3 bar and the part of the 2-to-3 bar at 2.9 or more: none of 200. Rare is not impossible.

figure.description: Bar graph (x-axis "Difference in means (cm) in 200 re-randomizations", y-axis "Count"). < -2: 0, -2 to -1: 29, -1 to 0: 74, 0 to 1: 66, 1 to 2: 27, 2 to 3: 4, ≥ 3: 0.

questions.prompt: In a randomized caffeine experiment, the caffeine group's mean reaction time was 0.04 s faster. Under the model that caffeine has no effect, 62 of 200 re-randomizations gave the caffeine group a mean at least 0.04 s faster. Using a one-sided count and a 5% cutoff, is the difference significant?
questions.prompt_markup: In a randomized caffeine experiment, the caffeine group's mean reaction time was 0.04 s faster. Under the model that caffeine has no effect, 62 of 200 re-randomizations gave the caffeine group a mean at least 0.04 s faster. Using a one-sided count and a 5% cutoff, is the difference significant?

choices.text: No: 62/200 = 31% > 5%, so the difference could easily be chance.
Yes: 62/200 = 31% is more than 5%, so the difference is significant.
No: 31% > 5%, and this proves that caffeine has no effect.
Yes: 0.04 s is less than 5% of a second, so it is significant.

questions.correct_answer: No: 62/200 = 31% > 5%, so the difference could easily be chance.
questions.grading_note: 31% is common. Not significant is not proof of no effect.

questions.prompt: What does a re-randomization simulation assume, and how is it carried out?
questions.prompt_markup: What does a re-randomization simulation assume, and how is it carried out?

choices.text: It assumes no treatment effect; each group's values are re-sorted from smallest to largest, and the two sorted lists are compared once to find the difference.
It assumes the treatment works; the observed difference is doubled and halved many times, and the results are graphed to show how large the effect could be.
It assumes no treatment effect; all responses are pooled and randomly re-split into groups of the original sizes, and the difference in means is recorded many times.
It assumes the treatment works; new subjects are recruited for each run, and the difference in their group means is recorded many times to estimate the true effect.

questions.correct_answer: It assumes no treatment effect; all responses are pooled and randomly re-split into groups of the original sizes, and the difference in means is recorded many times.
questions.grading_note: Null model plus shuffling of labels.

questions.prompt: Why is a difference between two group means compared with the variability in the groups?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is a difference between two group means compared with the variability in the groups?

choices.text: Any difference between the group means proves a treatment effect.
The variability in the groups gives the exact size of the effect.
A difference is meaningful only if it is large relative to the natural variation.
Variability matters only when the two group means are equal.

questions.correct_answer: A difference is meaningful only if it is large relative to the natural variation.
questions.grading_note: Signal versus noise. The others are false: a difference alone is not proof, variability is not the effect size, and variability always matters.
